beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: A slogan. It's the kind of line that goes on a 2017 slide.

beats.trigger: Revisit the crux, what would have to be true, pre-mortem.
beats.got: Homework from earlier modules I wasn't in. Not relevant to me.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: Learning objectives with verbs in bold. A strategy kernel in a two-week plan sounds like something I could actually use.

beats.trigger: The question to carry through: where is all this going?
beats.got: There's a shared folder and agents write into it. The 'question to carry' is a bit coachy.

beats.trigger: You watch one agent build another on real input. That's the whole lecture.
beats.got: Short and no pitch. I'll wait and see the demo.

beats.trigger: You describe an agent; the coding agent builds it.
beats.got: I describe a tool and the machine builds it, in 25 minutes.

beats.trigger: "On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand."
beats.got: Four lines about a gap. This is concrete. I have such a gap: the weekly partner pipeline summary my team compiles by hand.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: It built a working agent for my gap in fifteen minutes. That was not possible two years ago, so I'll give it that.

beats.trigger: "You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."
beats.got: I can push back and check the output against my files. That I can test myself, so I believe it more.

beats.trigger: The second agent next week takes ten, because your vocabulary for what you want is sharper.
beats.got: The speed-up is claimed, not shown. One run is not a trend. 'Not a new sprint' is a dig at agile, fair enough.

beats.trigger: The room's agents form a proposal forum around it
beats.got: Twenty people's agents argue with each other over a company challenge. Sounds like a workshop with extra steps.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: At least they know the legal problem exists. Our legal team would have questions about a shared folder.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Independent first opinions before the group sees each other's. Sensible, nothing new.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: Read your neighbours' notes and fix the gaps. Peer review.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: An audit trail of who changed their position. That's a mildly useful side effect.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: The prompt makes the synthesizer pick and cite, and mark it provisional. That's a rule I'd want.

beats.trigger: From here on, every agent prompt begins by reading `midway-instructions.md` from the shared folder.
beats.got: One central file steers all the agents mid-run. 'Injection' is the word our security people hate. Who controls that file?

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: Agents critique the draft selection. It's a review loop.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: A person decides which assumptions to test. Good. 'Show of hands, name it provisional' is how we already work.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: Three files at the end. A strategy doc, a list of agents and a plan.

beats.trigger: Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.
beats.got: The kernel has a risks section with an early warning sign. Better structure than most of our steering-group decks.

beats.trigger: "You are now agent builders. You have built agents that do real work on your company's data."
beats.got: Scripted identity ceremony. I am being asked to be excited, and I won't be. Nobody over 40 enjoys that.

beats.trigger: You do not graduate. You have a flywheel.
beats.got: Pure programme vocabulary, but I did like the line about it not converging on the first try. Pushback was the work.

beats.trigger: Four observations and two questions follow.
beats.got: A short lecture. At least it announces its own length.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The skill moves from building to specifying. That's an honest and sensible reframe, and it matches what I saw in the exercise.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Access isn't uptake, and I can count it myself on our own output. That's the first thing today that sounds like our last three rollouts, and the first that makes me think about whether it would stick here.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Agents make up sources unless forced to cite. A candid limit, and a rule I can check.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: Three obstacles to scaling. Data access is ours, and I assume it's everyone's.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: Flattering claim that what I did is the durable part. Unproven, and conveniently good for the course.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: They admit they don't know what will be obsolete. First time a training has said that to me, and it makes the rest more credible.

beats.trigger: If what your company knows stays flat, every model release widens the gap.
beats.got: The model improves for free and the company only improves if someone writes things down. True, and also the usual problem with knowledge management.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: Ask what would make us drop the plan. I'd use that on the last programme's roadmap too. Nobody could have answered it.

beats.trigger: nothing in the room checked it. Hold that doubt as you did then.
beats.got: They say the output was unchecked and I should stay doubtful. Candour again, though 'first turn of the flywheel' is the brochure voice.

beats.trigger: The prompt names the file before rewriting, quotes before-and-after for every claim, and surfaces stalls.
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites a file, with before/after quotes. Fine, a diff.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's self-assessment, and here is a question to test it. Right, I'd do that.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: Four bullets. Cite, check, expect obstacles, expect the model to change.

beats.trigger: You leave with a flywheel, not a graduation.
beats.got: Same closer again. I think the 'nobody has thought of it yet' line is honest, but the rest is a closing slide.

take_homes: Writing a clear description of the gap is the real skill, and the agent builds the rest. I watched it do that in fifteen minutes on my own pipeline summary.
Access to everyone's files is not the same as people using them. Count what the output actually cites before promising a board anything.
Ask what would make us drop the plan. If nobody can answer, it's a belief.

monday.move: Describe my weekly partner pipeline summary as a four-line brief, have the agent build it, and check its claims against our files.
monday.who: me, with one analyst from my team checking the output
monday.stop_condition: If the agent cannot cite a source file for each number, or the analyst has to redo more than half of it, I drop it.
monday.blocker: Customer data and the legal team's view on what may go into a US-hosted tool, plus a calendar full of steering groups.

misconception.why: A working agent for a real gap in fifteen minutes is something I couldn't have had two years ago, and the 'count the folders' and 'obsolete next year' lines were honest enough that this doesn't sound like the last programme. I still think the room ceremony is the old playbook, and I'm not yet convinced it won't blow over; I'd wait for one more demo on our data.

one_line: The build-an-agent exercise was real and the part about counting what people actually take up from each other was honest. I could have done without the 'you are now agent builders' ceremony and the flywheel talk.
